blocks.text: Think about your bank app for a second. It does not show you every single transaction from the last year the moment you open it. It shows you one number at the top: your current balance. That number is the end result of thousands of individual deposits and withdrawals, all collapsed down into a single value you can actually use. That collapsing, taking a pile of numbers and boiling them down to one representative value, is exactly what aggregation means in pandas.

blocks.alt: Many raw values flowing into an aggregate function and coming out as one summary number
blocks.caption: This is the entire idea behind every aggregation function.

blocks.text: 1. Introduction

An aggregation function takes many values and returns one value. sum adds everything up. mean finds the average. count tells you how many values there are. min and max grab the extremes. std tells you how spread out the numbers are. You have probably already used a basic aggregation without even thinking about it, calling something like df.groupby('region')['sales'].sum() to get a quick per group total. This lesson goes much deeper than that one line.

items: Aggregating an entire DataFrame with no grouping at all, for a fast overall summary.
Running several aggregations at once with a list.
Applying different aggregations to different columns with a dict.
Naming your result columns clearly instead of living with pandas messy defaults.
Writing your own aggregation function when the built in options are not enough.
The real difference between aggregation and transform.

blocks.text: 2. Aggregating a Whole DataFrame Without Grouping

Aggregation does not require a groupby at all. Sometimes you just want a quick overall summary of an entire DataFrame before you even think about splitting it into groups. How many rows total. What is the average price across everything. What is the maximum quantity ever ordered. For that you call the aggregation directly on the whole DataFrame.

code.content:
df.sum()
# quantity     1520.00
# price       48210.75
# dtype: float64

df.agg('sum')
# identical result, same values

blocks.text: Pandas applies the function to every numeric column separately and hands you back a Series, one entry per column. It does not sum quantity and price together into one grand total, it treats every column on its own.

blocks.alt: A whole DataFrame being summarized with df.agg sum with no grouping involved
blocks.caption: A fast overall summary before you even think about grouping anything.

blocks.text: 2.1 The Dedicated Method and agg Do the Same Thing

df.sum() and df.agg('sum') give you the exact same output. The dedicated methods like .sum(), .mean(), and .count() are really just convenient shortcuts. .agg() is the general purpose entry point that all of them funnel through underneath, and it is the one that unlocks everything else in this lesson: multiple functions at once, per column functions, and custom functions, all through that same single method.

code.content:
df.mean()
df.agg('mean')
# same output both times, mean is just a string name agg understands

blocks.title: Non numeric columns get skipped or complained about
blocks.content: If your DataFrame has a text column mixed in, calling something like df.sum() on the whole thing may either skip it, concatenate the strings, or raise an error, depending on your pandas version and the exact function. When you are aggregating a mixed DataFrame, it is safer to select the numeric columns you actually want first, or pass numeric_only=True.

blocks.text: 3. Multiple Aggregations at Once with a List

Calling .sum() gives you one number per column. But often you want several statistics side by side in one shot, the mean, the standard deviation, the minimum, and the maximum, without writing four separate lines. Pass a list of aggregation names to .agg() and pandas builds you a small summary table in a single call.

Notice the shape here. Each aggregation name becomes a row, each original column stays a column, and every cell is that statistic computed on that column. It is basically describe(), except you get to choose exactly which statistics show up instead of the fixed default set.

blocks.alt: Multiple aggregation names in a list producing a small summary table from a DataFrame
blocks.caption: One call, several statistics, one small table back.

blocks.text: 3.1 The Same List Trick on a Single Series

The exact same list syntax works on a single column too. Instead of a small table with columns down the side, you get back a Series indexed by the aggregation name, which is handy when you only care about one field.

code.content:
df['price'].agg(['mean', 'std', 'min', 'max'])
# mean    1205.27
# std      340.11
# min      599.00
# max     2100.00
# dtype: float64

blocks.text: 4. Different Aggregations for Different Columns Using a Dict

Here is the real power move. Most of the time you do not want the same statistic applied to every column, you want quantity summed and price averaged in the same call, because summing a price column does not mean anything useful. A dict lets you say exactly that: which column gets which function.

Each key in the dict is a column name, each value is the aggregation you want applied to just that column. Pandas runs sum only on quantity and mean only on price, then hands both results back together. This works exactly the same way after a groupby too, which is where you will use it constantly.

blocks.alt: A quantity column being summed and a price column being averaged then combined into one result
blocks.caption: Different columns, different functions, one dict, one call.

blocks.title: Every key needs to be a real column
blocks.content: If you misspell a column name inside the dict, or reference a column that was already dropped earlier in your pipeline, agg raises a KeyError immediately. It will not silently ignore a typo for you.

blocks.text: 4.1 Multiple Aggregations Per Column in the Same Dict
You are not limited to one function per column either. Make any dict value a list instead of a single string, and that column gets every aggregation in the list.

blocks.alt: A single price column having sum mean and max all computed from one dict entry
blocks.caption: One column, several functions, all listed together.

blocks.text: This is genuinely useful, but it is also exactly where the next problem shows up, because as soon as one column gets more than one function, pandas has to invent some way to label all those results, and its default choice is not pretty.
5. The Messy Default: Multi-Level Column Names

The moment you give a column more than one aggregation, whether through a dict or after a groupby, pandas cannot just call the result column price anymore, since there are now two price results. Its solution is a MultiIndex column header, a two level label like price mean stacked on top of price max.

blocks.alt: Two functions on the amount column producing a two level column header
blocks.caption: This two level header is the default pandas gives you, and it trips up almost everyone at first.

blocks.text: Try to grab one of those columns the normal way and you will hit a wall. summary['price'] gives you back a whole mini DataFrame with both mean and max still inside it, not the single Series you probably expected. You need the full tuple, summary[('price', 'mean')], or you need to flatten the columns yourself first.

code.content:
summary.columns = ['_'.join(col) for col in summary.columns]
# now: price_mean, price_max
summary['price_mean']  # works as a normal Series lookup

blocks.title: The multi level header is the single most common beginner trap here
blocks.content: New pandas users almost always hit this the first time they combine a dict of aggregations with more than one function on the same column. The fix above works, but there is a cleaner way to avoid the mess entirely from the start, which is exactly what the next section covers.

blocks.text: 6. Named Aggregation: Clean, Readable Column Names

Named aggregation lets you decide the output column name yourself, right there in the same call, instead of accepting whatever pandas invents. After a groupby, pass keyword arguments where the name you choose becomes the column, and the value is a tuple of the source column plus the function to apply to it.

code.content:
report = df.groupby('region').agg(
    total_sales=('amount', 'sum'),
    avg_order=('amount', 'mean'),
)
print(report)
#         total_sales  avg_order
# region
# east         18200.0     910.00
# west         24650.0    1027.08

blocks.text: Read that syntax left to right. total_sales is the name you want in the output. The tuple amount sum tells pandas exactly which column to read from and which function to run on it. No MultiIndex, no tuple lookups, no renaming step afterward. The column is called total_sales because you said so.

blocks.alt: Named aggregation producing clean single level column names instead of a multi level header
blocks.caption: Same idea as before, just with column names you actually chose yourself.

blocks.title: This is worth the extra typing
blocks.content: Named aggregation takes a few more characters to write than the dict shortcut, but the column names it produces are immediately readable by anyone who opens the result later, including future you. In a report or a dashboard, total_sales beats a MultiIndex tuple every single time.

blocks.text: 6.1 Combining Several Named Aggregates Across Columns
Named aggregation really shines once you start pulling statistics from several different source columns into one clean result, all in a single agg call.

Four different results, three of them pulled from amount and one from quantity, and every single column in the output has a name that tells you exactly what it means without opening the documentation.
7. Writing a Custom Aggregation Function

Sometimes none of the built in options do what you actually need. Maybe you want the range of a column, the biggest value minus the smallest one, and pandas does not ship a function called range. In that case you just write a normal Python function and hand it straight to agg.
Your function receives the whole column as a Series and has to return exactly one value. It works everywhere the built in names work too, inside a list, inside a dict, and inside named aggregation.
For something this small you can also skip the def entirely and reach for a lambda.

blocks.alt: A custom function computing the maximum minus the minimum of a price column
blocks.caption: When none of the built in names do what you need, you just write the function yourself.

blocks.title: The function must return a single value
blocks.content: If your custom function returns a Series or an array instead of one scalar, agg either raises an error or gives you a confusing result. Sum, average, count, whatever it is, boil it down to one number. If you find yourself wanting to return one value for every row instead, you are not writing an aggregation anymore, you are writing a transform, which is the topic of the next section.

blocks.text: 8. Aggregation Versus Transform

This is worth calling out clearly, because the two get mixed up constantly. An aggregation always collapses a group down to a single value. If you group ten rows and aggregate, you get one row back. A transform does the opposite job, it computes something using the whole group but hands you back a value for every original row, so your output stays exactly the same length as your input.

code.content:
df.groupby('region')['amount'].sum()
# one row per region

df.groupby('region')['amount'].transform('sum')
# one row per ORIGINAL row, the group total repeated on each of them

blocks.alt: Grouped data branching into an aggregate path returning one value per group and a transform path returning one value per row
blocks.caption: Same starting point, two very different shaped results.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Aggregation","Transform"],"rows":[["Output length","One row per group","One row per original row"],["Typical use","Building a summary table","Attaching a group stat back onto every row"],["Example call","groupby.agg sum","groupby.transform sum"],["What it enables","Rank regions by total sales","Compute each row's percent of its group total"]]}

blocks.text: You will get the full picture, including exactly when to reach for transform instead of aggregation, in its own dedicated lesson later in this module. For now, just remember the one line test: does your output need to be shorter than your input, that is aggregation, or does it need to stay the same length as your input, that is transform.
9. Worked Example: Building a Sales Summary Report
Put all of this together on something that looks like real data. Say you have raw sales rows, one per order, and you need a clean per region report for a Monday morning meeting.

The goal is one readable row per region: total revenue, the average order size, how many orders came in, the biggest and smallest single order, and total units moved. Named aggregation handles the entire thing in one call.

code.content:
report = df.groupby('region').agg(
    total_sales=('amount', 'sum'),
    avg_order=('amount', 'mean'),
    order_count=('amount', 'count'),
    max_order=('amount', 'max'),
    min_order=('amount', 'min'),
    total_units=('quantity', 'sum'),
).round(2).reset_index()

blocks.text: round(2) keeps the money columns from spilling into a dozen decimal places, and reset_index() pulls region back out as a normal column instead of leaving it as the index, which matters if you are about to export this straight to a CSV for someone else to open.

blocks.alt: Raw sales rows flowing through a group by region step and named aggregation into a finished summary report
blocks.caption: The full pipeline behind the worked example below.

blocks.text: Every column name tells you exactly what it holds, there is no MultiIndex to flatten, and the whole report came from one agg call instead of six separate lines glued together afterward. That is the entire point of learning aggregation properly instead of just memorizing df.sum().

blocks.alt: A summary report broken into total sales average order order count and max and min order columns
blocks.caption: Six clearly named statistics, all produced from a single agg call.

blocks.text: 10. Recap

items: An aggregation collapses many values down to one summary number: sum, mean, count, min, max, and more.
You do not need a groupby at all to aggregate. df.agg('sum') or df.sum() summarizes a whole DataFrame in one line.
Pass a list to agg for several statistics at once, producing a small summary table.
Pass a dict to apply different aggregations to different columns in a single call, the real power move.
Combining multiple functions on one column produces messy multi level column names by default.
Named aggregation, name equals a tuple of column and function, sidesteps that mess with clean, readable output columns.
Write your own function and hand it to agg whenever the built in options fall short, as long as it returns a single value.
Aggregation returns one row per group. Transform, covered in its own lesson later, returns one row per original row.
